realityCards.title: It's a highlight reel
realityCards.body: Most posts show someone's best moment from a whole week. You're comparing your everyday to their best 1%.
realityCards.tip: Next time you compare, add: "...but I'm only seeing their highlights."

realityCards.title: Filters and edits are everywhere
realityCards.body: Many photos are filtered, edited, posed or taken 50 times. Real skin has texture and real bodies change.
realityCards.tip: Try following a few accounts that show real, unedited life.

realityCards.title: The feed loves extremes
realityCards.body: Apps show whatever keeps people watching: the most perfect, shocking or dramatic content. That's not what normal life looks like.
realityCards.tip: Tap "Not interested" on content that makes you feel worse.

realityCards.title: Refreshing is by design
realityCards.body: Pull-to-refresh, likes and endless feeds work a bit like slot machines: you never know what's next, so you keep checking. That pull is the design, not a weakness in you.
realityCards.tip: Turn off notifications for apps you check too often.

realityCards.title: Perfect lives can be businesses
realityCards.body: Many influencers have sponsors, editors, lighting and a plan. It's work, presented as everyday life.
realityCards.tip: Ask: "Is someone being paid to make this look easy?"

realityCards.title: Nobody posts the boring bits
realityCards.body: Everyone has dull days, awkward moments and messy rooms. They just don't film them.

realityCards.title: Followers aren't friends
realityCards.body: A few people who really know you matter more than a big number of people who scroll past.
realityCards.tip: Message one person who knows the real you.

realityCards.title: You can't see their hard days
realityCards.body: People who look happy online can be lonely, stressed or struggling too.
realityCards.tip: Be kind in comments. You never know what someone is carrying.

realityCards.title: Compare with past you
realityCards.body: The only fair comparison is you versus you, a little while ago. What have you learned or survived since then?
realityCards.tip: Write one thing you can do now that you couldn't a year ago.

realityCards.title: FOMO fades
realityCards.body: Missing a post, trend or party feels huge in the moment. A week later, you probably won't remember it.

realityCards.title: Your worth isn't a number
realityCards.body: Likes, views and streaks measure attention for a few seconds. They don't measure who you are.
realityCards.tip: Try hiding like counts if your app allows it.

realityCards.title: AI can fake almost anything
realityCards.body: Photos, voices and videos can now be made or changed with AI. Seeing is no longer believing.
realityCards.tip: Check where something came from before you believe or share it.

realityCards.title: Real people look different
realityCards.body: People come in every shape, size, colour, ability and style. Feeds often show a very narrow slice.
realityCards.tip: Follow creators who look and live in many different ways.

realityCards.title: Online anger is louder
realityCards.body: A few loud voices can make it look like "everyone" thinks something. Most people are kinder in real life.
realityCards.tip: You don't have to join every argument. Muting is allowed.

realityCards.title: Game worlds are built to pull you in
realityCards.body: Daily rewards, loot, levels and streaks are designed by experts to keep you playing a bit longer.
realityCards.tip: Decide your stopping point before you start playing.

realityCards.title: Real life is slower, and that's okay
realityCards.body: Skills, friendships and confidence take time to grow. Fast rewards online can make real progress feel slow, even when it's happening.
realityCards.tip: Notice one small real-life win today.

guides.title: Block, report, save evidence
guides.summary: What to do when someone is mean, threatening or won't leave you alone online.

sections.heading: First: it's not your fault
sections.body: Nobody deserves to be harassed, threatened or embarrassed online. You don't have to reply, and you don't have to handle it alone.

sections.heading: 1. Pause before you reply
sections.body: Replying or getting back at them often makes things worse. It's okay to stay silent.

sections.heading: 2. Save evidence
sections.body: Before you block, keep a record so you can show someone later.
bullets: Screenshot messages, posts and comments, including the username and the date.
Copy links to profiles or posts.
Write down what happened and when. You can use Lumi's private evidence log.
Never forward or save sexual images of anyone under 18, even as evidence. Write down where they are and report them instead.

sections.heading: 3. Block or mute
sections.body: Blocking stops them contacting you. Muting or restricting hides them without them knowing. Both are allowed and both are smart.

sections.heading: 4. Report it
sections.body: On most apps you can tap the three dots (⋯), press and hold a message, or open the profile to find Report. Reports are usually anonymous.

sections.heading: 5. Tell someone you trust
sections.body: A friend, family member, teacher, coach or youth worker can help you decide what to do next. If you've been threatened or feel unsafe, contact emergency services or a helpline.

guides.title: Cyberbullying: spot it, stop it
guides.summary: What it looks like, how to respond, and how to help a friend.

sections.heading: What it can look like
sections.body: Bullying online is repeated behaviour meant to hurt someone.
bullets: Mean messages, comments or memes
Leaving someone out of chats on purpose
Spreading rumours or private information
Pretending to be someone else
Sharing embarrassing photos or videos

sections.heading: If it's happening to you
sections.body: Save evidence, block, report and tell someone you trust. What they do says something about them, not about you.

sections.heading: If it's happening to a friend
sections.body: Be an upstander, not a bystander.
bullets: Don't like, share or laugh along.
Message your friend privately: "I saw that. Are you okay?"
Help them report it or tell a trusted adult.
Report it yourself. Reports are usually anonymous.

sections.heading: If you've been unkind
sections.body: Everyone makes mistakes. Delete it, apologise if it's safe to, and think about what was going on for you. Talking to someone can help.

guides.title: Pressure for photos and image threats
guides.summary: If someone pressures you for intimate images or threatens to share photos of you.

sections.heading: It is not your fault
sections.body: If someone pressures you for nude or sexual images, or threatens to share images of you unless you do something (sometimes called sextortion), the person doing it is the one in the wrong. You can get help, even if you sent something before.

sections.heading: What to do right now
bullets: Stop replying. Don't send more images or money: it rarely makes them stop.
Don't delete the chat yet. Screenshot their profile, username and messages.
Block and report the account on the platform.
Tell a trusted adult or contact a helpline. People who work with young people deal with this often and want to help.

sections.heading: Getting images taken down
sections.body: Platforms remove intimate images shared without consent. Free services can also help: for under-18s, Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org) and for adults, StopNCII.org work with many platforms to stop images being shared.

sections.heading: Consent always matters
sections.body: Sharing someone else's intimate image without their consent is a serious harm, and in many places it is a crime. If someone sends you one, don't share it. Delete it and report it.

guides.title: Red flags in online friendships
guides.summary: Signs someone online may be trying to manipulate you.

sections.heading: Trust your gut
sections.body: Most people online are who they say they are, but some pretend in order to manipulate. These are warning signs, especially together:
bullets: Lots of compliments, attention or gifts very quickly
Asking you to keep the friendship secret
Wanting to move to a private or disappearing-message app
Asking for photos, your location or personal details
Trying to turn you against friends or family
Getting angry or guilt-tripping when you say no

sections.heading: What you can do
sections.body: You can stop talking to anyone, any time, without explaining. Save the chat, block, report and tell someone you trust. Never meet someone from online alone; if you do meet, choose a public place and bring a trusted adult.

guides.title: If you see something upsetting
guides.summary: Violent, sexual, hateful or self-harm content can show up unexpectedly. Here's what helps.

sections.heading: You can close it
sections.body: You don't have to finish watching. Close the app, look away, take a breath. Seeing it was not your fault.

sections.heading: Talk about it
sections.body: Upsetting images can stick in your mind. Telling someone you trust usually makes them feel smaller. The grounding exercise in Lumi can help if it keeps coming back.

sections.heading: Report and filter
bullets: Report the post so fewer people see it.
Tap "Not interested" or "Show less" to change your feed.
Turn on sensitive-content filters or restricted modes in your apps.
Mute words, hashtags or accounts that lead to that content.

sections.heading: Content about self-harm or suicide
sections.body: If you see content like this and it brings up difficult feelings, please reach out to someone. Use the Help button in Lumi any time.

guides.title: Scams and fake accounts
guides.summary: How to spot tricks that try to get your money, codes or accounts.

sections.heading: Common tricks
bullets: "You've won!" giveaways that ask for details or payment
Someone asking for a code sent to your phone
Free game currency or skins if you log in on a strange site
Urgent messages: "Act now or your account will be deleted"
A friend's account suddenly asking for money

sections.heading: Stay safe
sections.body: Never share passwords or login codes, even with friends. Check links before tapping. If a friend asks for money, check with them another way. If you've been tricked, change your password, tell someone and report it. It happens to adults too.

guides.title: AI fakes and edited images
guides.summary: Images, voices and videos can be faked. What to do if it happens to you.

sections.heading: Seeing isn't believing
sections.body: AI tools can create realistic photos, voices and videos of real people. Check the source before believing or sharing something shocking.

sections.heading: If someone makes a fake of you
sections.body: It's not your fault, and it's not okay. Save evidence, report it to the platform, and tell a trusted adult. Image-removal services like Take It Down (under 18) or StopNCII.org (18+) can help with intimate fakes.

sections.heading: Don't make or share fakes of others
sections.body: Even as a joke, fake images can hurt people badly and can be illegal.

guides.title: Digital consent and healthy relationships
guides.summary: Asking first, respecting no, and spotting controlling behaviour.

sections.heading: Ask before you share
sections.body: Before posting a photo of someone, tagging them, or forwarding their message, ask: "Is it okay if I share this?" A no is a no, and a yes can change later.

sections.heading: Healthy looks like
bullets: Respecting each other's privacy and passwords
Being free to have your own friends and time
No pressure to send photos or reply instantly
Feeling safe to say no

sections.heading: Controlling looks like
bullets: Checking your phone or demanding passwords
Tracking your location without agreement
Getting angry if you don't reply fast
Pressuring you to send photos

sections.heading: If something feels off
sections.body: You deserve to feel safe. Talk to someone you trust or a helpline. Use the quiz below to practise.

guides.title: Privacy check-up
guides.summary: A quick checklist to make your accounts safer. Tick things off as you go.

sections.heading: Why bother?
sections.body: The fewer strangers can see about you, the fewer chances they have to bother you. These settings are usually under Settings > Privacy in each app.

checklist.text: Set accounts to private (or friends only)
Choose who can message, comment or add you
Turn off location on posts and photos
Stop sharing live location with people you don't fully trust
Hide your online or last-seen status
Turn on tag and mention approval
Use different passwords for important accounts
Review which apps can use your camera, mic, contacts and location
Check old posts for things like your school, address or routine

guides.title: Keep your accounts yours
guides.summary: Simple habits that stop people getting into your accounts.

sections.heading: Strong and different
sections.body: Use a long passphrase (like four random words) and a different one for each important account. A password manager can remember them for you.

sections.heading: Codes are private
sections.body: Never share login codes or passwords, not even with a best friend or partner. Real companies never ask for them.

sections.heading: Shared devices
sections.body: Log out on shared or school computers, and don't let browsers save passwords there.

guides.title: How the scrolling trap works
guides.summary: Why it's so hard to stop, and what makes it easier.

sections.heading: It's designed this way
sections.body: Endless feeds, autoplay and notifications remove natural stopping points. Unpredictable rewards (a funny video, a like) make your brain want "just one more". It's not a lack of willpower.

sections.heading: Add stopping points back
bullets: Turn off autoplay and most notifications
Move tempting apps off your home screen
Use Lumi's pause screen or a daily limit
Try grayscale: colour makes apps more attractive
Set phone-free times for meals, study and sleep

sections.heading: Swap, don't just stop
sections.body: Scrolling often fills boredom, stress or loneliness. Having a ready swap (music, a walk, messaging a friend) makes it easier to put the phone down.

guides.title: Comparing yourself online
guides.summary: Why feeds can make you feel "not enough", and how to feel better.

sections.heading: Why it happens
sections.body: Humans naturally compare. Online, we compare our everyday lives to thousands of edited highlights, which isn't a fair contest.

sections.heading: Notice the feeling
sections.body: After scrolling, ask: "Do I feel better or worse?" Lumi's mood-after-scrolling check-in helps you spot patterns.

sections.heading: Shape your feed
bullets: Mute or unfollow accounts that make you feel bad (they won't know)
Follow people who inspire, teach or make you laugh
Hide like counts if you can
Use the reality-check cards when comparison hits

guides.title: When escaping goes too far
guides.summary: Stories, games and daydreams are good for you, until they replace your life.

sections.heading: Imagination is healthy
sections.body: Getting lost in a game, a show or a daydream can be fun and help you recharge. Needing a break from hard feelings is human.

sections.heading: Signs it might be too much
bullets: Losing sleep, skipping meals, school or plans to stay in it
Feeling worse, empty or irritable when you stop
Real life starting to feel unbearable in comparison
Using it to avoid a problem that keeps growing

sections.heading: Small steps back
sections.body: Set times for your favourite worlds, and add one small real-life thing you enjoy each day. If escaping is how you cope with something painful, talking to someone can really help.

guides.title: Why games are hard to stop
guides.summary: Game design tricks and simple ways to stay in control.

sections.heading: The hooks
bullets: Daily rewards and login streaks
Loot boxes and random drops (like gambling)
Battle passes with time limits
"Just one more match" with no natural ending
Friends waiting for you in a squad

sections.heading: Stay in control
bullets: Decide when you'll stop before you start
Use Lumi's session timer and "last round" warning
Set a weekly gaming budget
Stop at a natural break, not in the middle of a match
Avoid spending money when you're tired or upset
Notice how you feel after playing

sections.heading: When to get help
sections.body: If gaming causes problems with sleep, school, money or relationships, and you can't cut down even when you want to, talk to a trusted adult or a professional.

guides.title: Feed spring-clean
guides.summary: Mute and unfollow reminders to make your feed kinder.

sections.heading: A 10-minute clean-up
bullets: Scroll your following list. For each account ask: "Does this make me feel better or worse?"
Mute or unfollow the "worse" ones. Muting is invisible.
Mute words or hashtags that upset you.
Tap "Not interested" on content you don't want.
Follow 3 accounts that make you laugh, learn or feel inspired.

sections.heading: Make it a habit
sections.body: Feeds drift over time. A monthly clean-up keeps them working for you.

checklist.text: Muted or unfollowed accounts that make me feel worse
Muted words or hashtags I don't want to see
Followed a few accounts that inspire me

guides.title: Peer pressure online
guides.summary: Challenges, group chats and pressure to post. How to say no.

sections.heading: You can say no
sections.body: Dangerous challenges, pile-ons in group chats, or pressure to share something private: you never have to join in.

sections.heading: Easy ways out
bullets: "Nah, not for me."
"My phone's dying, gotta go."
Leave or mute the group chat
Blame Lumi: "My app has a limit on, sorry!"

sections.heading: Find your people
sections.body: Real friends respect your no. If a group keeps pushing you, it's okay to spend less time with them.

guides.title: Sleep basics
guides.summary: Simple habits that help most people sleep better. Not medical advice.

sections.heading: Wind down
sections.body: Screens, bright light and exciting content make your brain think it's daytime. Try putting screens away 30 to 60 minutes before bed.

sections.heading: Habits that help
bullets: Similar bedtime and wake time each day, even at weekends
Phone charging outside the bedroom
Daylight in the morning
Less caffeine after lunch
Write worries down before bed

sections.heading: If sleep is hard for weeks
sections.body: Talk to a trusted adult, a doctor or a health professional. Long-lasting sleep problems are common and can be helped.

guides.title: Understanding stress
guides.summary: Stress is normal. Here's how to bring it down a notch.

sections.heading: Your body's alarm
sections.body: Stress is your body getting ready for a challenge: fast heartbeat, tight muscles, racing thoughts. A little helps you perform. Too much for too long wears you out.

sections.heading: Three kinds of tools
bullets: Body: slow breathing, movement, muscle relaxation
Mind: break big tasks into tiny steps, write worries down
People: talk to someone, ask for help with what's too much

sections.heading: When to reach out
sections.body: If stress or worry stops you sleeping, eating, going to school or seeing people for a while, please talk to someone. You deserve support.

guides.title: Beating procrastination
guides.summary: It's about feelings, not laziness. Tricks that make starting easier.

sections.heading: Why we put things off
sections.body: We avoid tasks that feel boring, confusing or scary. Phones give instant relief, which makes avoiding even easier.

sections.heading: What helps
bullets: The 5-minute start: promise yourself just 5 minutes
Make the first step tiny: "open the document"
Phone in another room or Lumi focus mode on
Work in short sprints with breaks
Be kind to yourself. Guilt makes avoiding worse

consentQuiz.scenario: A friend posts a group photo and tags you without asking. You hate how you look.
consentQuiz.explanation: It's okay to ask them to untag you or take it down. Asking before posting others is the kind default.

consentQuiz.scenario: Your partner says that if you really trusted them, you'd share your password.
consentQuiz.explanation: Trust doesn't need passwords. Pressure like this is a sign of control.

consentQuiz.scenario: Someone sends you a screenshot of a private chat about a classmate and says "pass it on".
consentQuiz.explanation: Sharing private messages without consent can hurt people. Don't pass it on.

consentQuiz.scenario: Your close friend and you agree to share live location on the way home from a late event.
consentQuiz.explanation: Agreed, temporary location sharing with someone you trust can keep you safe. You can stop any time.

consentQuiz.scenario: Someone you like keeps asking for a private photo after you said no.
consentQuiz.explanation: No means no. Repeated pressure is never okay. You can block, report and tell someone.

consentQuiz.scenario: You want to post a funny video of your friend. You ask first and they say yes.
consentQuiz.explanation: That's consent. And if they change their mind later, take it down.

Went for a walk with my cousin instead of gaming all evening. Didn't expect it to feel that good.
Feeling flat this week and I'm not sure why. Writing it here because saying it out loud feels like too much.
Any tips for stopping late-night scrolling? I tell myself "one more video" for an hour.
Home gets loud sometimes. Headphones and the breathing exercise are how I cope. Sharing in case it helps someone.

replies.text: It took me a whole term to find my people. Joining a club helped way more than I thought.
Thanks for sharing this. Starting somewhere new is hard, and it's really common to feel this way at first. Have a look at the Events tab for clubs and groups. You're not alone.
I turn on grayscale after 10pm. Makes everything way less interesting!
Charging it across the room helped me. If I want to scroll I have to get up.
Sending you strength. Flat weeks happen and it's brave to say it.
Same! I do 25 minutes on, then a short break. Way easier.

note.author: Someone in my class keeps posting jokes about me in a group chat. I don't want to make it a big deal.
note.helper: Thank you for telling us. That sounds really unfair, and it's not your fault. You don't have to handle it alone. It might help to save screenshots in Lumi's evidence log and think about who you'd feel safe telling. We're here if you want to talk it through. (Demo reply.)
